_README: Approach variants, batch J — 21 routes, 29 variants, every one carrying a baseFinding.
Delivered without `area` on any entry, which enrich:apply refuses. `area` is filled in here from
the live rows by scripts/oneoff/finalize-approach-batch-J.mjs rather than typed, because six of
these ids carry no peak name at all (wa_east_ridge_9 = Ingalls East Ridge, wa_ne_ridge = Cathedral
Peak in the Pasayten, wa_east_face_6 = Chimney Rock, wa_mount_maude_r1/_r2) and a name-shaped id
is not evidence of which peak you are on.
Contamination rejected during research, recorded so it is not re-introduced: Chimney Rock's
'West Face / Rappel Chimney' is IDAHO (Selkirk Crest); a Mount Maude bergschrund description
referencing the Haig Glacier is in the Canadian Rockies; Cathedral Peak in Tuolumne shares a route

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda Basin trailhead, Ingalls Way over Ingalls Pass to Lake Ingalls
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep once the slabs above the lake are clear; snow lingers below the notch into early summer
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Esmeralda Basin trailhead (about 4,240 ft) at the end of the North Fork Teanaway road, FR 9737. A free self-issue Alpine Lakes wilderness permit is filled out at the register.

There are TWO forks and published beta routinely runs them together. The first comes at roughly a quarter to half a mile, where the old mine-road grade splits: bear RIGHT onto Ingalls Way #1390. Straight on is Esmeralda Basin #1394, a different valley. The second fork is higher, around 5,600 ft and roughly a mile and a half in: RIGHT climbs to Longs Pass, which is a viewpoint and the way toward Ingalls Creek and Stuart's south side, not a way to this climb. Stay LEFT.

From there the trail traverses steadily to Ingalls Pass at about 6,500 ft, where Mount Stuart and the Ingalls group come into view all at once. Continue about another mile to Lake Ingalls, roughly 6,400-6,480 ft and about 4 miles from the car. This is the last water.

From the lake, work up and climber's-left on Class 2-3 slabs, talus and boulders. Stay with the cairned line. Parties who leave it for a more direct-looking line get cliffed out; one recorded downclimbing past a waterfall to escape.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The target is visible from the lakeshore: the cleft between the North and South peaks, with a single pointed spire sitting in it. That spire is the Dogtooth. Aim just left of it and let it draw you up the slabs.

At the Dogtooth, go RIGHT for the traditional approach gully. The last gully is scree. If the gully you are in is green and lush it is the wrong one and it will carry you too high — traverse right out of it onto clean scree.

Arrival is physical: a short section of Class 4 up a crack of roughly forty feet at the top of the gully lands you on a ledge. That ledge is where the rope comes out. Pitch one is the low-angle slab above it, taking the large crack system up the middle.

Touch test at the start: the rock here is green serpentine, an odd slick band quite unlike the surrounding granite, sitting just up from the Dogtooth crag. Large hexes work in it where cams skate. Confirmation higher up — the pitch-three ledge carries two big bolts and there are three more at the top.

NEGATIVE MARKER, and this is the one that matters. This route climbs the south ridge of the NORTH peak, and the North peak (7,662 ft) is the true summit. The South peak (7,640 ft) is a separate Class 3 scramble that starts from the SAME notch. If you reached the notch, dropped about fifty feet down its west side and scrambled easy gullies back to a top without ever roping up, you climbed the South peak. That is not this route and not the high point.

Second marker: finishing the technical pitches does not put you on the summit. There is a few hundred feet of walking left to tag the actual high point, so a summit that arrives the instant the climbing ends is the wrong one.
hazards: Cliffing out on the slabs above and beside the lake if you leave the cairned line for a direct one
Loose talus and scree in the approach gully with parties above
Afternoon thunderstorms on a wholly exposed ridge — start early
A 60 m rope does not reach on the descent rappels, roughly fifteen feet short; carry a 70 m or doubles

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Way Alternate #1390.2 through Headlight Basin (the camping branch)
approach_variants.season: Same window; this is the branch to take if you are sleeping out, since camping at Lake Ingalls is prohibited
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to Ingalls Pass. Just past the pass the trail splits and the right-hand branch is signed Ingalls Way Alternate #1390.2. It drops into Headlight Basin, crosses Headlight Creek, and holds the established campsites and the reliable water. The main #1390 stays high along the rim of the basin and is the more direct line to the lake.

The two rejoin at a signed junction less than a quarter mile below Lake Ingalls, so this costs you a descent and a re-ascent in exchange for a legal camp and running water. Parties climbing the same day generally take the high line; parties camping take the low one.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This branch does not change where the climbing starts — it rejoins the standard line at the signed junction below the lake, and from there the Dogtooth, the scree gully and the forty-foot Class 4 crack onto the belay ledge are exactly as on the high route.

What it does change is your starting view. Coming up out of Headlight Basin you meet the lake from below rather than from the pass, so you will not have had the long look across at the peak that the high traverse gives you. Walk to the lake outlet and pick out the notch and the Dogtooth spire from there before starting up the slabs, rather than trying to identify them mid-scramble.
hazards: Headlight Creek crossing
Braided use paths through the basin camps — stay on durable ground, this is Alpine Lakes Wilderness
Extra descent and re-ascent on the way out with a full pack

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda Basin trailhead to Lake Ingalls, then the north-east notch gully
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the approach gully holds snow well into summer and is often climbed on snow
approach_variants.notes:
Drive and walk exactly as for the South Ridge: Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of FR 9737, right at the low fork onto Ingalls Way #1390, left at the higher fork where Longs Pass branches off, over Ingalls Pass at about 6,500 ft, and on to Lake Ingalls at roughly 6,400-6,480 ft, about 4 miles and the last water.

The two routes part company ABOVE the lake. Skirt the lake on its left (west and north) side and cross a band of slabs to reach a large talus gully. A boot path shows itself in patches through the talus. This gully runs more directly than the South Ridge slabs and is steeper and looser — expect Class 2-3 scree with real rockfall potential if anyone is above you.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the east ridge of the NORTH peak, and the notch it starts from is the one on the far side of the summit from the South Ridge — between the North peak's eastern terminus and the separate East peak. Two obvious gullies rise off the ground above Lake Ingalls to two different notches on the same mountain, and choosing between them is the whole navigational problem here. The South Ridge's gully leads to the notch between North and South; this one leads round to the north-east side.

Going up, the arrival test is a change in the rock rather than a change in angle. Climb the obvious gully — usually snow early in the season — until you reach an odd, anomalous rock layer that does not match what you have been walking over. From there move about fifteen feet LEFT and you are at the base. An alternative published description of the same spot has you looking RIGHT for a smaller third-class gully and starting where it stiffens into easy fifth-class rock; either way the marker is the change in the rock underfoot, not the height on the ridge.

Confirmation once you are moving: there are slings with rap rings at the top of the first pitch, used as the belay for the second. If you climbed a rope length and found nothing fixed, doubt the start.

Touch test: the rock through here is serpentine — greenish, slick, and quite unlike granite friction. That slickness is normal for this peak and is not a sign you are on harder ground than intended.

POSITIVE MARKER that reads like a mistake: a couple of pitches up, after passing a mid-sized gendarme on its right, you are forced to downclimb about twenty feet of fourth class into a notch in the ridge. That downclimb is correct here and is evidence you are ON the East Ridge, not that you have gone wrong. The easy knife-edge traverse midway along is the same kind of confirmation.

The descent is the South Ridge rappels, ending at three bolts at the top of that route — so the 60 m rope warning from the South Ridge applies to this climb too even though you never touch its approach.
hazards: Steep loose talus in the approach gully, worse with parties above
Lingering snow in the gully into midsummer
No water above Lake Ingalls
A 60 m rope comes up short on the shared South Ridge rappel descent

approach_variants.name: Stuart Lake trailhead and the Mountaineer Creek valley to the 5,400 ft basin
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug; the ice cliff and the couloir exit get harder and more broken as the season runs on
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, about 3,400 ft. Follow the main trail to the first fork, roughly two and a half to three miles in near 4,600 ft, and stay RIGHT for Stuart Lake. Left is Colchuck Lake, a different basin on the other side of the ridge.

About a mile past that junction — one source says a mile and a half — the Stuart Lake trail turns uphill and swings right, away from the water, and begins switchbacking. That turn is your cue. Leave the trail there and stay flat in the valley bottom with Mountaineer Creek. The test is simple and works in poor visibility: if you are gaining elevation on switchbacks you are walking to Stuart Lake and you have missed it.

Cross Mountaineer Creek on logs. There is no single canonical log and reports describe several sporty crossings that shift with the snowpack; early season, snowbanks make dropping onto a log awkward.

On the far side, pick up the climbers' path along the creek. It is unmaintained, full of blowdown and re-routes, and the cairns are not to be trusted: they invite you up and right into a boulder slope around 4,675 ft. Two independent accounts say stay LOW beside the creek instead, with the creek on your left — the path is unpleasant but the better line. Some parties do use the boulder field deliberately to avoid the creek crossings, so treat it as a documented disagreement rather than a mistake.

After about a mile and a half the valley steepens. Turn right and west and climb talus and forest into a hanging flat basin at about 5,400 ft, under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers. That right-turn-and-climb out of a steepening valley into flat ground is the arrival cue for the bivy.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE NORTH RIDGE ROCK RIB IS THE DISCRIMINATOR, not the look of the ice. Standing in the 5,400 ft basin facing the mountain, in order from your left: Sherpa Glacier, then Ice Cliff Glacier, then the enormous rock rib of the North Ridge, then the Stuart Glacier beyond it.

So: if that rib is on your RIGHT, you are on the Ice Cliff. If you have walked around the rib and it is now on your LEFT, you are on the Stuart Glacier and have gone too far west. If there is no hanging ice anywhere above you and the slope is a uniform moderate angle, you are on the Sherpa and have gone too far east.

The name is the second test. Ice Cliff is the only one of the three carrying a hanging ice cliff and serac band partway up. Sherpa has none.

The move itself: walk the moraine up to the FOOT of the North Ridge, then cut hard LEFT and traverse east under the ice cliff at about 6,600 ft. You are aiming under the cliff, not up the rib.

TOUCH TEST at the base, and it is unmistakable in cloud: the ground is not clean snow. It is frozen avalanche debris mixed with fallen chunks of glacier ice, set solid — a talus field made of snow and ice. Standing on that is direct evidence you are underneath the ice cliff.

Both the far left and the far right side of the icefall are used, and which one goes is a conditions question rather than a route question. The same is true of the bergschrund: one published description passes it on the climber's right, another on the left. Do not treat either as fixed, and look before committing.

Exit: surmounting the cornice puts you on the south-facing ridge just BELOW the false summit near 8,600 ft. Standard descent is the Sherpa Glacier, immediately east of the couloir exit, starting around 8,200 ft and dropping back into the same basin — so a party reversing the Ice Cliff is doing something unusual.
hazards: Serac fall from the hanging ice cliff you traverse beneath — a party watched a large piece break away and shatter on the ledge below them
Rockfall and avalanche in the couloir
Crevasses and thin snow bridges on the lower glacier
A cornice at the couloir exit, which becomes the crux when large
An unmaintained climbers' trail with blowdown and misleading cairns
Sporty log crossings of Mountaineer Creek, worse under early-season snow

approach_variants.name: Early-season approach with the Eightmile road gated
approach_variants.season: Spring, roughly Apr-May, when the route is in as snow and ice
approach_variants.notes:
When Eightmile Road is snowed or gated below the trailhead, add roughly two and a half miles of road before the trail proper. Parties walk that stretch and then put skis on, skinning the Stuart Lake trail, before continuing on foot.

This is a genuinely different day rather than a longer walk: the valley is snow-covered, the log crossings may be buried or may be harder to reach off a snowbank, and the boulder-field-versus-creek question largely disappears under snow. Postholing on the cross-country section is the common complaint.

No reliable published trailhead-to-bivy time exists for either version, so plan from your own pace rather than from a number.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The identification is the same and the North Ridge rib is still the thing to steer by — Sherpa left, Ice Cliff centre, the rib on your right, Stuart Glacier beyond it.

What changes in spring is that the frozen-debris touch test at the base may be buried or covered by fresh avalanche deposit, so it is less useful. Fall back on the geometry: you want to be under the ice cliff with the North Ridge rib immediately to your right, having cut left off the moraine at the foot of the rib rather than continuing up alongside it.
hazards: Avalanche on the approach slopes and in the couloir
Buried or unreachable log crossings
Deep postholing once off skis
Extra road mileage each way when the gate is down

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake trail and the PCT, then the Chimney Creek climbers' path to the moraine basin
approach_variants.season: Early summer is better than late here. As the season runs on the glacier opens up and the moat at the foot of the rock becomes the thing that turns parties around
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Pete Lake trailhead off Cooper Lake Road, FR 46 then FR 4616. Published trailhead elevations run from about 2,790 to 2,900 ft depending on who you read, so do not treat any one figure as exact. A Northwest Forest Pass is required and this is Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Bikes are allowed on roughly the first two and a half miles of trail and no further.

Walk the Pete Lake trail #1323 up the Cooper River, about four flat forested miles to Pete Lake, then on past the lake staying left at the forks to meet the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT roughly a mile to a mile and a half.

The turn-off is a landmark, not a mileage, and four independent sources describe it the same way: the trail crosses an old avalanche swathe at about 3,360 ft and switchbacks sharply. Stop at that hairpin and look west across the valley. Twin waterfalls come down out of a hanging basin — that meltwater is coming off the Chimney Glacier and that basin is where you are going. To the right of the falls are two rounded rock outcrops and further right a cliff band; the climbers' path goes up the forest BETWEEN the rounded outcrops and the cliff band. One account puts its start at an obvious logjam giving creek access, only about twenty yards inside the forest rather than the two hundred a guidebook suggests. Orange flagging appears in places and should not be relied on.

One recorded wrong turn on that path: it climbs north-west and runs up to a rocky gully. Do not go up the rocky gully. The line continues LEFT through vine maple and bracken fern, where the tread is buried under a season's growth.

The path crosses three ravines, the second being the awkward one, and reaches bivy ground below the moraine. Reports name a rock buttress above the waterfalls as Sunrise Knob at roughly 4,650 to 4,700 ft; another party camped in a meadow at about 4,800 ft. Times from the car to that camp are reported anywhere from four and a half to over six hours, and a Mountaineers profile suggests planning three days for what many parties attempt in two.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the bivy the thing to identify is the U-Gap, the notch that almost every party climbing this peak passes through. Chimney Rock is the second peak to the RIGHT of the U-Gap. Fix that relationship from camp, in daylight, before you are on the glacier.

Getting onto the upper glacier is a three-way choice and every source lists the same three: a rock or snow gully in the cliff band just left of the icefall (the usual, described as grungy and wet), a snow finger far to the left, or the icefall climbed directly if you have screws and the conditions for it.

THE MOAT IS THE ARRIVAL, and whether you can get from snow onto rock at all is the crux of the day rather than a formality. Parties describe reaching the bergschrund at the foot of the face and finding it large, then getting across only because fallen ice blocks had tumbled in and built a ramp and platform to step off. If there is no such ramp there may be no way onto the rock, and that is a condition of the season, not a route-finding failure.

Above the U-Gap the traverse across the South Peak toward the Main Peak is a sequence of ledges that one party fairly called improbable — the first of them begins about fifteen vertical feet BELOW the U-Gap on its east side, so a search at gap level finds nothing.

NEGATIVE MARKER worth carrying: Beckey's description of a blind chimney on the way to the broad ledge under the summit tower was found by one party to be a very loose, dangerous, grungy gully. They backed out of it and instead downclimbed about fifty feet from the Main Notch and picked up an obvious reddish third-to-fourth-class ramp leading to the small notch they wanted. If you are grovelling in rotten grunge you are probably in the feature they abandoned.

A final sanity check on how rarely this is done: the summit register suggests roughly one party a year. Do not expect a boot track or fresh tat to confirm anything for you.
hazards: The moat and bergschrund at the base of the east face, which can be impassable late season
Crevasses on the Chimney Glacier and an active icefall between the lower and upper sections
Very serious route-finding — a well-known serious fall on this peak happened off route
Loose rock throughout the summit ledges and gullies
Vine maple and bracken burying the climbers' path, and flagging that may lead nowhere
Mosquitoes heavy down at lake level

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake and the Chimney Creek climbers' path, then straight up the glacier under the summit
approach_variants.season: Early summer. Late in the year the moat under the face is the problem rather than the climbing
approach_variants.notes:
The walk in is the same as for the East Face and is described in full there: Pete Lake trail #1323 up the Cooper River to Pete Lake, on to the Pacific Crest Trail, then roughly a mile of PCT to the hairpin in the old avalanche swathe at about 3,360 ft. Look west from that hairpin for twin waterfalls; the climbers' path leaves the forest between the two rounded outcrops right of the falls and the cliff band right of those. Camp below the moraine at roughly 4,650 to 4,800 ft.

From camp, drop about two hundred feet to the lower Chimney Glacier, rope up, and cross it. Gain the upper glacier by the rock or snow gully in the cliff band just left of the icefall, by the snow finger out on the far left, or by the icefall itself if you are equipped for it.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route and the ordinary East Face part company on the upper glacier, and the difference is where you aim.

The Direct does NOT go to the U-Gap. Once on the upper glacier, keep going up until you are on the east face of the MAIN peak, directly beneath the summit — you want the summit vertically above you, not a notch off to one side. That position is the whole identification.

The arrival test is the moat that forms there. It is the gate: you are looking for a place where fallen ice has bridged or filled it enough to step from snow onto rock. If you find yourself traversing sideways along the base looking for a way in, that is normal and expected here.

NEGATIVE MARKER: if you have climbed to a notch on the skyline and are now working across ledges on the SOUTH peak toward the main summit, you have taken the U-Gap and you are on the ordinary East Face, not the Direct. That is a perfectly good climb, but it is not this one.
hazards: The moat directly under the summit, whose passability is a seasonal accident
Icefall between the lower and upper Chimney Glacier
Crevasses on the glacier
Loose rock on the face
A long, poorly-tracked approach where the flagging is unreliable

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Pass trail #1345 from the Cle Elum River road end
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct. Early season, with the gullies still snow-filled, the rockfall hazard is lower — this is the rare Cascade route that is arguably safer under snow
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Cle Elum River Road, SR 903, to Salmon La Sac, then keep right just past the ranger station onto the rough Forest Road 4330 and follow it about twelve miles to the road end at roughly 3,350 ft.

There are TWO trailheads within a few yards of each other at the road end and this is the first place to go wrong. The Hyas Lake and Deception Pass trail heads NORTH. You want the Cathedral Rock trail, #1345, heading WEST, and it may be signed slightly before the road actually ends. Vehicle break-ins have been a recurring problem at this trailhead, which is a pattern rather than a one-off.

The trail reaches Squaw Lake at about two and a half miles and continues to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, roughly four miles in with about 3,400 ft of gain. Turn LEFT, west, onto the Pacific Crest Trail. In less than half a mile you reach the junction with Trail #1375 to Peggy's Pond.

At that junction two climbers' paths head toward the peak, and the counter-intuitive one is the right choice: the LEFT path looks from a distance like the wrong way, but it avoids a scree slope and gives some scrambling instead. Either goes, but do not talk yourself out of the left one on appearances.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The handrail is elevation plus one named feature. Follow the scramble gully on the RIGHT side of the rounded spur upward until the spur runs into the summit formation at about 6,400 ft. That contact point — where broken spur ground ends against continuous rock — is where the approach stops and the climb starts.

From there the line is the obvious gully on the upper LEFT, to the left of the South Buttress. If the buttress is on your left you have gone too far right; the buttress should be to your RIGHT as you enter the gully.

One recorded refinement inside that gully, which is around a hundred yards long: stay right at first and cross left higher up, scrambling on rock, rather than taking the centre — the middle holds the loose rock and the steeper steps.

One to two pitches of the southwest face above the gully reach the ridge crest, and most parties rope up for that even though it is graded fourth class. From the crest it is a short scramble to the top.

What is NOT here, and the absence is worth saying: there is no famous single wrong gully at Cathedral Rock. The published hazard is rockfall and loose rock, stated repeatedly and in plain terms. The genuinely wrong-start stories on this peak are all from the Northeast Buttress, a different route on the other side, so do not import them.
hazards: Serious rockfall in the summit gully, the peak's named hazard, worst with parties above
Loose rock on the summit scramble as well as in the gully
Picking the Hyas Lake / Deception Pass trailhead by mistake at the road end
Vehicle break-ins at the trailhead
Braided use paths across the meadows near Cathedral Pass

approach_variants.name: Peggy's Pond, gaining the summit gully from the ledge above the pond
approach_variants.season: Same window; the ledge traverse into the pond is nastier with a heavy pack or under snow
approach_variants.notes:
Walk to Cathedral Pass as for the standard, then continue on Trail #1375 to Peggy's Pond. The final half mile or so into the pond is primitive, crossing narrow ledges with real exposure, and it feels harder than anything on the maintained trail before it.

Peggy's Pond is the last reliable water and the last established camp, so this is the variant for parties splitting the day or combining the climb with Mount Daniel.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the pond you gain the same summit gully, but from below and on the south side rather than by traversing in from the pass. Climb to the ledge above the pond and follow it to the foot of the gully system.

The identification is unchanged: you want the gully to the LEFT of the South Buttress, entered where the spur ground dies against the continuous summit rock near 6,400 ft. Coming from the pond you meet that rock from underneath, so the check is that the buttress stands to your right as you turn up into the gully.
hazards: Exposed narrow ledge traverse on the way into Peggy's Pond
Rockfall in the summit gully
Snow lingering on the pond ledges into early summer

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake and the PCT, leaving the trail at the Lemah Creek footbridge
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep; the chute below the summit is easier as snow than as loose rock, so earlier is often better
approach_variants.notes:
Walk the Cooper River trail #1323 about four flat miles to Pete Lake, then roughly another mile and a quarter past the lake staying left at every fork to meet the Pacific Crest Trail. Turn onto the PCT and follow it about a mile to Lemah Creek.

The trail-leaving cue is sharp and three sources give it: LEAVE THE TRAIL BEFORE THE FOOTBRIDGE over Lemah Creek. There is a campsite at the bridge. If you have crossed the creek on a bridge you have gone past it. Note that sources disagree about whether the Lemah junction is north or south along the PCT from Pete Lake, so navigate to the bridge itself rather than to a compass direction.

A faint path climbs the creek side past waterfalls — Whinnimic Falls is the big one — and within about twenty minutes the ground opens onto rocky knobs. The valley floor above is flat and marshy at around 3,700 ft. Continue roughly a mile and more up the valley to the marshy basin under the long snow gully that starts on the north side of Lemah Five.

Two lines lead from that basin up to the Lemah Glacier and neither is obvious from the marsh; one of them carries significant brush. Where the gully melts out at a waterfall, it is better to stay RIGHT and return to snow above than to scramble the left side. Leave the gully onto heather around 4,800 ft.

One further note on names: Lemah has five summits and the MAIN one is the MIDDLE, Lemah Three. Beta that talks about Lemah Two is talking about a different top on the same ridge.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The arrival is a rock step, called a chute in the guidebooks, and it sits below the main summit after you have crossed the glacier basin and traversed north under Lemah Two.

The touchable sequence at the step, from a party who did it: pass a small waterfall, climb a wet gully for about ten feet, then work RIGHT onto dry rock. Those ten feet are the fourth-class move and the landing beneath them is relatively safe. That waterfall-then-wet-gully-then-step-right is the thing to look for; it is the crux of the whole climb and it is where the approach ends.

There is a tempting alternative that does not work: a ramp far to the LEFT looks as though it would let you bypass the rock step entirely, but reaching it means an unpleasant moat crossing, and the party that looked at it came back down and took the step.

ABOVE the step, the recorded mistake is worth more than the recorded route. Between Lemah Two and Lemah Three there is a small snowfield. A guidebook sketch puts the line just left of the summit rocks, and following that into a mostly snow-filled gully leads to a difficult top, a snow bridge onto loose rock, and about a hundred feet of loose third and fourth class. The party who did that found on the way down that the honest instruction is simply: gain the ridge where it looks easiest. It is.

One route people have taken and should not repeat: descending a gully from Lemah One to reach the glacier. It melts out into very unstable talus blocks.

The Spectacle Lake approach is documented but has been explicitly superseded — the slide area between the lake outlet and the shoulder has grown into ten- to twelve-foot slide alder on a thirty-degree slope, dense enough that you cannot see over it to aim at anything.
hazards: Cold, sometimes thigh-deep creek crossings in the Lemah valley early season
Brush and blowdown on an unmaintained, lightly-used path
The moat beside the rock step
Loose rock on the final hundred feet if you take the gully rather than the ridge
Very poor rock quality generally — this ridge is chossy even by Cascade standards

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake and the PCT switchbacks to the Vista Lakes tarns
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, but see the moat note — the gate at 7,000 ft can shut by mid-July, earlier in a thin snow year
approach_variants.notes:
Walk the Pete Lake trail #1323 up the Cooper River to a fork at about 3,120 ft, roughly five miles in. Turn right, continue about six tenths of a mile, and turn right again onto the Pacific Crest Trail at about 3,220 ft. Follow the PCT four and a half miles up a long series of switchbacks to about 5,500 ft.

The Vista Lakes tarns lie east of the trail at that height and hold the good bivy sites. Summit Chief is about two more miles from there. Reported times from the car to the upper lake run to most of a day with overnight loads, and every published account treats this as a two- or three-day trip.

This is also the last reliable water. The ground above is reported bone dry until you come back down to the lakes.

From camp, leave the PCT and traverse cross-country toward Summit Chief Pass, then follow the ridge north-west staying BELOW the cliffs and gendarmes, into the upper basin south-east of the main summit. One party's hindsight on this traverse is worth having: they should have dropped to about 6,000 ft and taken the scree instead of holding height across steep sloping slabs.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is a specific chain of features here and it ends at a piece of ground that is unmistakable once you know to look for it.

From the upper basin, find a small NOTCH in the skyline ridge to the west. To reach it, head north-west toward a MINOR ROCK RIDGE that runs west-south-west to east-north-east across the base of the summit. That minor ridge IS the base of the climb — arriving at it is arriving.

Gain it by the snow in the gap at its RIGHT, LOWER end, then walk along the top of the ridge to the notch at its WEST end. On the far side of the notch is a steep gully, usually icy in the morning, and beyond that a loose-rock gully; the exit is the gully on the right just below the summit.

NEGATIVE MARKER, learned the hard way and independently corroborated: from the snowfield below the south-east face, the FIRST and LEFT-MOST snow finger leading to the south ridge is a dead end. It runs into a deep notch and the party that took it had to retreat. Go instead to the UPPER RIGHT corner of the snowfield, exit onto steep dirt and scree, and pick up a left-slanting ramp to a higher notch. Two separate accounts arrive at the same instruction from opposite directions.

THE MOAT IS THE GATE and it has a date on it. Where the mountain rises in earnest at about 7,000 ft a moat forms, and it may be impassable after mid-July, perhaps earlier in a low-snow year. If it stops you, there may be Class 3 rock in the middle of the basin as an alternative, but plan the trip around the calendar rather than hoping.

Do not trust a single photograph for the crossing point on the south ridge; parties report the pictures circulating online do not match the ground.

The top five hundred feet is steep dirt and thoroughly untrustworthy rock — one climber said it had earned honorary Olympic Mountains status. That looseness is normal for this summit and is not a sign you have wandered onto harder ground.
hazards: A moat around 7,000 ft that can close the route outright after mid-July
Icy gully beyond the notch in the morning — crampons are worth carrying for it
Steep dirt and very loose rock on the final five hundred feet
Rockfall from parties above on the hardpan and talus below the notch
No water at all above the Vista Lakes
Sloping slabs on the traverse from camp, avoidable by dropping to the scree around 6,000 ft

approach_variants.name: Lemah Meadow shortcut, cutting the PCT switchbacks
approach_variants.season: Same window; the bypass is brushier and is a trade of distance for thrashing
approach_variants.notes:
A recorded variant that saves about three miles. After gaining roughly a thousand feet on the tight PCT switchbacks, leave the trail at the corner around 4,000 ft and head north, climbing about six hundred feet to the crest.

The party who did it found plenty of windfall and pockets of vine maple, and called it irritating rather than difficult. It is a single-source variant, so treat the line as a hint rather than a route.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The shortcut rejoins the standard line on the crest above and does not change where the climbing starts. Everything from the upper basin onward is as for the standard approach: the skyline notch to the west, the minor rock ridge running west-south-west across the base of the summit, the snow gap at its lower right end, and the moat around 7,000 ft as the real gate.

What you lose by taking it is the view of the peak that the PCT switchbacks give you on the way up, so identify the minor ridge and the notch from the basin rather than expecting to have already picked them out.
hazards: Windfall and vine maple on the bypass
No tread and no cairns
Same moat and loose-rock hazards above

approach_variants.name: Dingford Creek, bike the closed road, then ford the Middle Fork under the big cliff
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The river ford is the timing constraint — thigh deep in the morning has been recorded as waist deep on the same day by evening
approach_variants.notes:
From I-90 exit 34 go north, then right onto SE Middle Fork Road, FR 56, and follow it about twelve miles to the Taylor River junction. Bear right onto FR 5620 and continue to the Dingford Creek trailhead at roughly 1,500 ft. FR 56 is notorious for potholes and ruts and high clearance is genuinely useful; the stretch beyond the gate is reported to be in better shape than the public road.

FR 5620 is decommissioned beyond Dingford Creek. Published figures for that closed stretch to the old Dutch Miller Gap trailhead and Hardscrabble Horse Camp are seven, eight and ten miles depending on the source, so do not plan on a precise number. A bike is universally recommended and cuts hours off both ends.

Beyond the road, published accounts diverge into three genuinely different lines and none of them corroborates another, so read all three before choosing.

The most specific of them fords the Middle Fork on a visual cue rather than a mileage: walk roughly four miles of trail until you can SEE the large cliff rising above the south side of the river at the foot of Overcoat. Push through about ten minutes of alder, ford there, and you land on the talus field at the base of those cliffs. Further north-east the alder gets much thicker. A second account crosses about a mile before the Dutch Miller Gap trail proper and climbs steep forest to camp at Overcoat Lake. A third crosses the river on rocks, climbs steep brushy ground into a two-mile rocky corridor its author calls the Valley of the Chiefs, meets continuous snow around 4,600 ft, and goes over a pass at about 6,140 ft.

On the traverse toward camp, one party's correction: they climbed to the ridge and then realised the line stays LOWER, and had to drop back to find the sloping rock crux and downclimb to the snow.

A durable warning about the road rather than the mountain: the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road has a long-standing reputation for unsavoury activity, including gunfire, and at least one regular visitor reports it on every trip.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The snow finger is not visible until you are underneath it, so do not try to identify it from camp or from the glacier below.

The sequence that works: reach the Overcoat Glacier, make a long rising traverse of five hundred feet or so to the top of the mild glacier, and only then does the steep snow finger show itself, with dark towers standing above it.

THE DARK TOWERS ARE THE TRANSITION. You leave snow for rock at their foot, then round the corner EAST and the glacier reappears below you. From there it is steep gully climbing on solid holds with a few exposed steps over tall blocks to the summit.

The consistent fact across every published account, and the one to steer by: the summit pyramid is gained on its EAST or NORTH-EAST side. Nobody describes climbing it from the south-east. If you are working around to the south side of the block looking for a way up, you have gone the wrong way round.

Grade opinions on that finish run from Class 3 to low fifth, and parties have pitched it out in two short pitches with a few small cams and nuts, with one rappel and some downclimbing to get back to the top of the snow finger. Expect thin protection and poor rock rather than a scramble.

Moats around the glacier margin and crevasses part way up the snow finger are the two things that most often force a detour here, and both were reported as more awkward than expected by parties who had read otherwise.
hazards: A real ford of the Middle Fork Snoqualmie, thigh to waist deep and colder in the afternoon than the morning
Dense slide alder on both banks, worse to the north-east of the standard crossing
Moats around the margin of the Overcoat Glacier
Crevasses part way up the snow finger
Poor protection and loose rock on the summit pyramid
A long decommissioned road walk or ride at both ends of the day

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col
approach_variants.season: Best while the face still holds continuous snow and ice, roughly Jun into mid-Jul; it used to hold year round and no longer does
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, roughly twenty-four miles and turn right onto the Phelps Creek road, FR 6211, to the trailhead at about 3,500 ft. The trail up the valley is the same tread hikers use for Spider Meadow, so trail-condition reports about it are usually not written by climbers.

Walk the Phelps Creek trail, #1511, about three and a half flat miles to where it meets Leroy Creek near 4,120 to 4,140 ft. Cross on a large tree or by rock-hopping — awkward in early season with the creek up — and pick up the well-worn but unsigned climbers' trail, #1512, on the north side of the creek. Some sources call this the Carne Mountain High Route and others treat the two as different paths, so do not assume the names are interchangeable.

It climbs steeply, then eases into the Leroy Creek Basin meadow at about 6,100 ft, roughly five miles from the car and a little over two hours for a party moving well with light packs. Good camping and water.

Above the basin, one party continued on the high-route path less than a quarter mile and then went directly into the upper basin below Maude by way of a gully with a small waterfall. Keep climbing cross-country over meadow, scrub, talus and probably snow to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col at about 8,150 ft, north-west of Maude's summit.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL IS NOT THE ROUTE, and that is the thing to internalise before you get there. From the col you have to go DOWN about four hundred feet, and not in one clean line — it comes in a series of forced descents alternating with traverses.

The recorded sequence: from the col, take the option toward the Entiat River valley side, downclimb roughly a hundred feet of face to a moderate bench, traverse a couple of hundred yards, be forced down again, traverse again, and eventually arrive at a steep snow slope beneath an overhang. That slope is the steepest ground of the day, around sixty degrees for the first moves, easing above.

THE TEST IS VISUAL AND IT IS UNAMBIGUOUS: you have descended far enough when the face comes into FULL VIEW. Until it does, you are still traversing. One party took an hour and a half from the col to standing on continuous snow at the foot of the face.

Once on it, the lower face runs around thirty-five to forty degrees. A rib on the right side of the face is the line parties choose, not because it is named but because it keeps you out from under the cornice.

WHAT NOT TO EXPECT: a bergschrund. The 1957 first ascent, coming from below on the Ice Lakes side, stood at a schrund between the glacier and the ice sheet above. Parties arriving by the col traverse enter partway up the face and bypass that ground entirely, and modern reports of this approach do not mention a schrund at all. The hazard people actually record here is the CORNICE at the top — one party had a piece of it come down and sweep across their tracks.

Honest gap worth knowing: nothing published tells you how to distinguish Maude's north face from Seven Fingered Jack's. The two, with Fernow, form one continuous headwall at the head of the Entiat, so the col is your positional anchor rather than the look of the wall.

On the way down, stay SOUTH and descend toward Ice Lakes. Parties regularly drop into one of the gullies cut into Maude's west side, either by mistake or thinking it a shortcut, and it is not.
hazards: Cornice at the top of the face — parties have had pieces release across their tracks
Four hundred feet of exposed descending traverse from the col on snow, ice and very loose Class 3
Sixty-degree snow for the first moves off the traverse
Leroy Creek crossing running high in early season
Very poor rock quality throughout this group of peaks
Descending a west-side gully by mistake instead of continuing south toward Ice Lakes

approach_variants.name: Entiat River and Ice Lakes from the east — the first-ascent line
approach_variants.season: Same window; this side is a much longer walk and is mostly used by parties already camped at Ice Lakes or exiting that way
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Entiat River Road and walk the Entiat River trail #1400 about eight and a quarter miles to the Ice Creek trail. The Entiat River has to be crossed on logs, and if there is no log at the trail there may be a large jam south of it.

The first-ascent party did not follow the river to the meadows at its head. They walked instead to the col between Spectacle Buttes and Maude's south-east side and dropped from Ice Lakes onto the slopes beside the face, judging it more direct and free of bushwhacking. That cost them nearly three thousand feet of climbing to reach Ice Lakes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base-finding here is one moment rather than a sequence: after the long grind up to Ice Lakes, you come over the crest and the face is right there in front of you. The first-ascent account says exactly that — the doubts about having picked the right way vanished on cresting the ridge.

Coming from this side you meet the face at its FOOT rather than partway up, which is the real difference from the col approach. That means descending steep snow slopes to a snowfield, then up to the glacier, and standing at the bergschrund between the glacier and the ice sheet above — around two thousand feet of it on the first ascent, averaging forty to forty-five degrees and over forty-five near the top.

So the test is which problem you are handed. If you are looking up at a schrund at the bottom of the whole face, you came from below. If you never saw one, you came across from the col.
hazards: Unbridged crossing of the Entiat River on logs
Bergschrund at the foot of the face on this side
A very long walk in on a trail that has burned in the past
Cornice at the top of the face

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin to a bivy at Icy Lake, then the notch onto the Entiat Glacier
approach_variants.season: Late summer for the ice, roughly Jul-Aug; the icefall has receded a long way and how much of it is climbable varies year to year
approach_variants.notes:
Approach as for the North Face: Phelps Creek trailhead, the Phelps Creek trail to the Leroy Creek crossing, then the unmarked climbers' trail up the north side of Leroy Creek into the basin, and on up toward Ice Lakes. Sources spell it Icy Lake as often as Ice Lakes; it is the same water.

Parties bivy on ledges above the south side of the lake, below the South Ridge. That is the sensible camp because the South Ridge is the descent — but be clear that it puts you on the WRONG SIDE of the mountain for this route, so the morning starts with a long traverse over a cliff band to reach the access notch. One party set themselves a turnaround rule of two hours from camp to the notch, on the grounds that any slower and there would not be time to finish.

Cross the talus above the lake to the notch that lets you onto the Entiat Glacier. Rope up and descend to find a short crossing through the ablation zone of the receding glacier — this is harder than the old guidebook photograph suggests. Skirt below the rock spur and head up toward the icefall.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE NOTCH IS THE THING YOU CAN GET WRONG, and there is a documented decoy. The access notch is at about 7,200 ft. A climbers' path leads to a DIFFERENT notch at about 6,900 ft, and a party who took it for the right one paid for the error with a long detour in the wrong direction up an ugly scree bash. If the notch you have reached is around six-nine rather than seven-two, keep going.

Once through the correct notch and onto the glacier, the sequence is: descend, cross the ablation zone, pass under the rock spur, then work RIGHTWARD beneath the headwall. Arrival at the climbing is a change in the ice — you move from walking to big crevasses with short vertical steps, and above those the angle relaxes to about thirty-five degrees of ice running up to the base of the rock.

That base of rock is the second, unmistakable transition: roughly nine hundred feet of fourth and low fifth class above it, with several ramps to choose between. Take the line of least resistance trending slightly toward the ridge crest. The rock is crumbly and protection is scarce, so running belays are the usual method rather than pitching it. There is a distinctive step-across at the top of a couloir partway up.

A note on how much ice you will actually find: in a heavy snow year one party bypassed roughly two pitches of the icefall on steep snow slopes off to the side, and the whole icefall took them an hour of running belays where they had budgeted six. Do not plan the day around a pitch count from an older description.

Descent is the South Ridge, which took that party half an hour — which is exactly why the camp is where it is.
hazards: A decoy notch at about 6,900 ft that leads to a long scree detour
Crossing the ablation zone of a receding glacier, trickier than published photographs show
Big crevasses with vertical steps in the icefall
Crumbly rock with scarce protection on the nine hundred feet above the ice
A long traverse over a cliff band from the Icy Lake camp before the route even starts

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek to Leroy Basin, then the couloir toward the Maude col
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep; a snow gully out of the basin may want an ice axe early in the season
approach_variants.notes:
From the Phelps Creek trailhead at about 3,500 ft, walk the Phelps Creek trail roughly three and a half miles to the Leroy Creek crossing at about 4,140 ft. One published source says two and a half miles; three others say three and a half, so treat the shorter figure as the outlier.

Immediately after the crossing, turn right onto the unmaintained climbers' trail on the north side of the creek. It gains roughly two thousand feet in about a mile and a half of steep, sometimes brushy boot tread and is the hardest sustained work of the day. It levels into the flat Leroy Basin meadow at about 6,100 ft, which is the standard camp, with reliable water.

Round trip for the peak is commonly given as about thirteen miles with 5,600 ft of gain, a figure two independent parties record.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the basin the terrain opens and the way up is genuinely apparent — this is one of the rare peaks in the group where the route reveals itself. Take the obvious couloir leaving the basin eastward, toward the saddle between Seven Fingered Jack and Mount Maude.

The sequence of touchable landmarks above that, in order: climb to the BASE OF CLIFFS at about 7,200 ft, then cut RIGHT to a BENCH at about 7,800 ft — you can reach the same bench more safely by coming at it from further south. From the bench, traverse steep scree northward staying BELOW the summit spires. Keep following the base of the spires until, near the top, you reach a DEEP NARROW RAVINE. Cross that ravine at its TOP, not lower down, and a climbers' trail from there takes you to the summit.

There is a second, more direct line out of the basin some parties use: a boulder field and a west-facing gully to the south shoulder at about 8,000 ft.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS AT THE TOP AND IT IS EXCELLENT: the true summit is the NORTHERN-most crag, which from the basin side reads as the LEFT-most hump. A climber in a whiteout climbed what looked like the highest thing, found it was not the summit, climbed the next crag north, found that was not either, and only the third was. Here is the test — the true summit crag is Class 2-3, and the two false crags to the SOUTH of it are HARDER, at Class 3. So if the crag you just climbed felt like the most difficult thing you had done all day, you are on a false summit and the real one is further north.
hazards: Uniformly loose rock and scree on the whole upper mountain — this group has a bad reputation and deserves it
Party-inflicted rockfall in the couloir out of the basin; small parties are strongly preferable
A lingering snow gully in the entry couloir early season
No shelter above the basin and no defined trail, so poor visibility makes the spires-and-ravine sequence much harder
Steep, brushy climbers' trail gaining two thousand feet out of the valley

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin, over the col and across the Gloomy Glacier
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing runs through avalanche terrain earlier than that
approach_variants.notes:
Same walk in as for Seven Fingered Jack and Maude: Phelps Creek trail to the Leroy Creek crossing at about 4,140 ft, then the steep unmaintained climbers' trail on the north side of the creek into Leroy Basin at about 6,100 ft.

This is the common approach but not the elegant one. It exists because the alternative is the ferry up Lake Chelan to Holden and the Railroad Creek trail into Copper Basin, which gains the East Ridge — the standard route — much more directly. A third option starts at Cottonwood on the Entiat River and reaches the East Ridge by way of the Entiat Glacier. All three converge on the same south-east face finish.

From Leroy Basin, head north-west toward a waterfall and climb its left side to a small notch on the ridge of Seven Fingered Jack. Published descriptions of this saddle vary — one places it just west of an obvious 7,700 ft col with a couple of bivy sites at the low point, another gives it as a notch reached past a second creek crossing — and they may or may not be the same feature, so check it on a map rather than assuming.

From the saddle you must DROP about a thousand feet into the moraine at the terminus of the Gloomy Glacier, and every foot of it has to be regained on the way out. Two published ways down: descend to the tarn below and go around a prominent rock formation that guards the basin, or descend to the right across sandy ledges and down large boulders.

Expect roughly nine hours round trip from Leroy Basin, and a very long day car to car — one party left the trailhead at three in the morning and got back at eleven at night.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FERNOW IS NOT VISIBLE FROM LEROY BASIN, and this is confirmed rather than folklore. Parties climbing the basin under the cirque of Seven Fingered Jack report having real difficulty identifying the route because the peak simply is not in view. Do not stand in the basin trying to pick your line off the mountain; you cannot see it. Carry a track.

The arrival test is short and physical: cross the moraine below the Gloomy Glacier, go UP THE WATERFALL, and you are in the broad basin below Fernow. That is where the climbing starts.

Above that basin there are two decision points and both have a wrong answer that is on record.

FIRST: descend the glacier to its terminal moraine at about 6,500 ft, then climb the RIGHT side of a stream to an upper snow-filled basin, and from there go south-west up a broad gully that turns eastward. That is Class 2-3 and, in the words of the climber who wrote it up, gives you the luxury of knowing where you are. The alternative — dropping only to 7,000 ft and making a rising traverse through a succession of gullies, ribs and small cliffs — is Class 3-plus with snow and ice and the feeling of being lost somewhere in the Entiat Mountains.

SECOND, and this is the one that matters: from the broad gully, DO NOT go all the way to the col and traverse the south-east face on the narrow ledges there. They are described as exposed enough to frighten a bird, with the honest observation that a fallen body would be unlikely to be found. Instead climb the broad gully to about 8,400 ft, then a loose gully to about 9,000 ft, and traverse the face at NINE THOUSAND on a wide ledge that is not exposed at all.

The 8,400 ft mark is a real landmark rather than a number on a map — two independent parties record the ground changing character there, one of them at a large bench holding permanent snow with water running off it. From 8,400 the line goes up loose talus to the ridge between Seven Fingered Jack and Fernow, where cairns pick up and weave around to the south-east ridge of the summit block. The cairns are reported by three separate parties, though one notes they stop near the summit itself.

The general principle behind all of it: climb as far as you can up the ridge separating Fernow's south-east and south-west faces. Once on the East Ridge, a couple of hundred feet of Class 3 on reasonably solid rock finishes it.
hazards: A thousand feet of descent into the Gloomy basin that must be regained on the way out
Avalanche terrain on the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing
Icy forty-degree slopes near the top of the Gloomy Glacier, with crevasses below the usual line
Two thousand feet of exceptionally loose talus and scree above the basin
The narrow exposed ledge traverse off the col, which is avoidable and should be avoided
Route-finding is the crux — this is regarded as the most complex of the three Entiat nine-thousanders

approach_variants.name: Trinity to Buck Creek Pass, then the High Pass high route around the west side
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the traverse from the Berge saddle crosses steep heather that is nasty when wet, and holds snow into summer
approach_variants.notes:
Start at Trinity at the end of the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, at about 2,800 ft. Take the Buck Creek trail #1513, which splits off the Chiwawa River trail within the first mile and climbs steadily to Buck Creek Pass — roughly six hours and about 3,100 ft of gain.

Why this way round at all is worth understanding before you commit: Buck sits only about three miles from Trinity as the crow flies and is Class 2-3 from the south-west, but a long rugged ridge runs north and south of it and there is no road or trail up the Napeequa on the west, so the normal route is a very long way round. The two documented ways to reach that west side are the high route north from Buck Creek Pass and Little Giant Pass from the south.

At the pass there is a large established camp with toilets just before the switchbacks up toward Liberty Cap. FILL UP WITH WATER THERE — there is none for the next four miles and the ridge walk is fully sun-exposed.

Follow the old High Pass trail as it winds high around the side of Liberty Cap, then south for several miles until the tread dies out in talus and hard snowfields at High Pass; crampons are worth having for that. Contour through the pass and under Mount Berge, then angle up to the ridge crest just south of Point 7839. A short section of Class 3 reaches a faint saddle from which there is an easy walk-off down into Louis Creek Basin.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The critical instruction on the traverse is about HEIGHT, and it comes with a stated consequence: from the saddle south of Berge, curving right around the bowl toward the mountain, STAY HIGH. Drop too low and you end up in steep waterfall slabs. If you are looking at running water over slabby ground, you have lost too much elevation and should climb back.

The arrival is unmistakable and it is not rock: you reach a beautiful forested bench with larches — good enough that parties note it as a campsite — and CROSS A RIVER. Once across that river you are at the base of Buck.

Above there the ground is broad pumice, talus and low-angle snowfield up to the south ridge around 7,400 ft, and then rubbly slabby schist along the crest with a short step up to Class 3-4 near a horn close to the top.

SUMMIT WARNING, and it is a genuine unresolved disagreement rather than a caution: published accounts do not agree how many summits Buck has or which is highest. One party climbed the middle of the long crest, found the register there, and judged it higher than both the north point and the south by twenty feet or more. Another says the south is the true one. A third found the register — dated 1967 — on the NORTH horn and reported the two tops as roughly equal. Only one of those parties actually measured anything. The summit crest holds several bumps within a few feet of each other, so expect to walk the crest rather than to arrive at an obvious high point, and do not treat a register as proof.

A useful sighting cue from a party approaching by a different line: the summit does not come into view until you reach the flat ground around 8,000 ft, in an upper cirque one climber described as looking like the flying bridge of a boat.

This mountain has killed someone — a climber fell fifty feet scrambling on a route on the east side, direct from Trinity, in 2018. The direct east line involves a river ford and a savage brushy bushwhack and is generally recommended as a descent rather than an ascent.
hazards: No water for four miles beyond Buck Creek Pass on an exposed ridge
Steep heather ledges at the Berge saddle, very sketchy when wet
Waterfall slabs below the traverse line if you lose too much height
Hard snowfields at High Pass wanting crampons
Loose rubbly schist on the summit crest, with a fatal fall on record on this peak
Burn scar on the lower Buck Creek trail — hot, and blowdown

approach_variants.name: Boulder Creek and the sheepherder's trail to the south basin — the non-glacier line
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jun-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the White River trailhead at the end of White River Road, FR 6400, at about 2,300 ft; a Northwest Forest Pass is needed. Walk the White River trail #1507 about four flat miles — one party gained all of three hundred feet in a little over an hour — to the Boulder Creek trail #1562 junction.

Turn east up Boulder Creek. At about the 5,000 ft level, roughly four and a half miles up this trail, pick up an old sheepherder's trail heading west and follow it to around 5,600 to 5,700 ft. Note that published mileages on this stretch do not reconcile cleanly between sources, so navigate by elevation and by the basin rather than by a mile count. There is a faint path that contours, crosses the creek and climbs the west side of Boulder Creek, firming up into decent tread as it gains the slope.

Leave the sheepherder's trail in the basin above Boulder Creek around 5,700 ft and climb open heather north-north-west to the southern ridge running off Clark's south-east peak, Point 8373.

Car to summit is given as about eleven and a half miles one way with roughly 6,500 ft of gain, and essentially every party camps in the Boulder Creek basin rather than trying it in a day.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
EVERYTHING TURNS ON ONE FEATURE AND IT IS MISDESCRIBED BY ITS OWN NAME. Guidebook language calls it the one and only easy gully breaching the ridge — the way down off the spur into Clark's south basin — and it leaves the crest at about 7,200 to 7,300 ft.

The correction, from a climber who found it: it is Class 2, and it FEELS MORE LIKE A SLOPING LEDGE THAN A GULLY. Parties hunting for a defined cleft walk past it and get cliffed out. Two independent sources both put it at 7,200 ft and both anchor it to the south spur of Point 8373, so the elevation is the reliable half of the identification and the word gully is the unreliable half.

The positional cue that puts you in the right place to look: there is a flattish section of the spur at 7,200 ft that is reached easily on scree and grass. Stand on that flat and you can see the south slope of Clark, which looks easy — and it is. The difficulty is purely in getting DOWN to it, which is what the ledge is for.

Drop a couple of hundred feet down that ledge, then contour the upper south basin on broken rock and patches of permanent snow to the final south ridge and a short Class 3 scramble to the top.

A note on names before you cross-reference anything: the Walrus Glacier is shown as the Clark Glacier on maps. They are one feature with two names.
hazards: Getting cliffed out on the spur while looking for a gully that is really a ledge
Unbridged Boulder Creek crossing, cold and thigh-deep early season and sometimes braided
Losing the sheepherder's trail — it is notoriously hard to find from the White River trail
Heavy mosquitoes on the valley walk
No water above the Boulder Creek basin

approach_variants.name: Boulder Pass and the Walrus Glacier — the glacier line
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jun-Sep, on the earlier side while the crevasses are still bridged
approach_variants.notes:
Approach identically to Boulder Basin: White River trail #1507 four miles to the Boulder Creek trail #1562, then up into the open basin at roughly 5,300 ft, about five to six hours and three thousand feet from the car. That basin is the camp.

From camp, climb north-east to Boulder Pass at about 6,300 to 6,330 ft. Drop down steep snow on the far side, then climb to a bench at about 6,700 ft on Clark's eastern arm.

THE BENCH IS WHERE YOU ROPE UP. Do it there, before you go anywhere, because of what comes next.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU CANNOT SEE THE WALRUS GLACIER UNTIL YOU ARE COMMITTED TO IT. From the 6,700 ft bench you wrap around Clark's eastern arm, and only then does the glacier come into view for the first time. That is why the bench is the roping-up point rather than the glacier's edge — there is no convenient stopping place once you are round the corner.

The entry is specific and it is not the middle of the toe: go up a moderately steep chute on the LEFT, SOUTHERN margin of the glacier. Expect to step over several narrow crevasses and, in at least one recorded year, to cross a snowbridge over a large one.

Once on the gentle upper glacier the summit wedge is visible in the distance and the navigation problem is over. The finish skirts the upper south face of that wedge on a steep snowfield and ends with a short scramble onto the summit rocks — about six hours from camp.

NEGATIVE MARKER, and this one matters because it would send you to the wrong landmark entirely: the famous one-and-only-easy-gully at 7,200 ft belongs to the SOUTH BASIN route, not to this one. If you are on the Walrus you never touch it. A published page titled for the Walrus Glacier in fact describes the south-basin line in its turn-by-turn, so read carefully which route a description is actually walking.
hazards: Crevasses and snowbridges on the lower Walrus Glacier
Steep snow on the far side of Boulder Pass
No view of the glacier until you have committed around the eastern arm
Unbridged Boulder Creek ford lower down
The 7,200 ft south-basin gully is a landmark for a different route and will mislead you here

approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; snow lingers at Andrews Pass into early July
approach_variants.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,080 ft, roughly a five-hour drive from Seattle and the shortest drive of the three ways in.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles pass through an old burn, so there is little shade and the tread can be overgrown and wet after rain, but the creek is beside you and reliable. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

Continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Published figures for the whole walk from this trailhead are about nineteen miles with 5,550 ft of gain, and everyone splits it over at least two days.

Of the three trailheads this one has the shortest drive and the most walking gain; the Thirtymile trailhead is only about five and a half miles further along the same road, which makes a car shuttle between them easy.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking approach from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the fines are severe.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THERE IS NO CLIMBERS' TRAIL TO THE BASE. A party who got there reported finding none and navigating purely off photographs, so stop looking for tread and navigate by the landform.

The landform is the deep gully that separates Cathedral Peak from The Monk, the semi-detached tower on the lower right side of the south face. One published account leaves the maintained trail at the FIRST SWITCHBACK after Cathedral Pass and heads for the gully from there; others come across the parkland between Upper Cathedral Lake and the pass. Both end up in the same place, thirty to sixty minutes from camp.

Go UP INTO the gully — do not stop at its mouth. Three independent sources put the start of the first pitch about 150 FEET UP the Cathedral–Monk gully, on the LEFT wall, which is the Cathedral side. Scramble onto a TALL PEDESTAL there; it gives a decent belay stance to start from. Pedestal, left wall, about 150 feet in: that is the whole identification.

HOW TO TELL THIS FROM THE SOUTH FACE ROUTES, and it is a simple physical test: is there a semi-detached tower standing between you and the wall? If yes, you are at the SE Buttress, which follows the ridge behind The Monk on the right-hand edge of the south face. If you are walking up to an open face with nothing in front of it, that is the South Face route, a different and much harder climb.

A related trap in the naming rather than on the ground: The Monk has its own south face with its own routes on it. Beta headed South Face may be describing the tower, not the mountain.

Coming down, the descent is the walk-off to the west and then south-west back toward Upper Cathedral Lake, and its crux is a gap the guidebook tells you to hop across. It can be avoided by downclimbing the exposed nose beside it and stepping over — easy when dry, but no-fall ground.
hazards: No climbers' trail to the base; navigation is off the landform and photographs
Long approach through burn with little shade and overgrown tread
A no-fall step-across or hop on the walk-off descent
Remote enough that a two- to four-day trip is the norm, so a retreat is slow

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
This is a TRAIL, #510A, and not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to the Iron Gate spur, a different road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then NF-39 and NF-300 to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print as Cathedral Driveway, Chewuch, and Chewack Driveway, and the Chewuch name also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not the name.

The Cathedral Driveway descends from its trailhead to join the Chewuch trail #510 around mile 4.8 at about 4,300 ft, and from there it is the Chewuch valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. Total is about seventeen and a half miles with roughly 3,700 ft of gain — the shortest walk and the least climbing of the three approaches.

The catch is at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead sits high and the trail drops to meet the Chewuch, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way OUT, at the point when you least want it.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The approach changes but the base does not. From camp at Upper Cathedral Lake it is the same thirty to sixty minutes: cross toward the deep gully dividing Cathedral Peak from The Monk, go about 150 feet up INTO the gully, and start on the LEFT wall from a tall pedestal.

What this approach does affect is your first sighting. Coming down the Chewuch you arrive in the basin from below rather than over Andrews Pass, so take the time at the lake to pick out The Monk as a separate tower leaning against the peak's flank before walking up. The tower in front of the wall is the whole discriminator between this route and the South Face, and it is far easier to identify from across the water than from underneath.
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip on the way out
A trailhead with four different published names
Same lack of any climbers' trail to the base

approach_variants.name: Upper Cathedral Lake camp, then the grassy south-east slope onto the ridge
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Reach Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft by any of the long trails — Andrews Creek #504 is the shortest drive, the Cathedral Driveway #510A the shortest walk, Thirtymile via the Chewuch #510 the middle option. All are multi-day and all put you in the same basin.

From the Boundary Trail below the peak, this route does not go into the Cathedral–Monk gully at all. Scramble up the grassy south-east slope directly from the main trail to gain the ridge.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are aiming for the long broken ridge that runs between Cathedral Peak and The Pope, a separate small peak further north along the same crest, sitting right on the Canada–United States border.

That relationship is the base-finding and it is also the warning. The ridge has a peak at each end. If you keep working north along the crest past the point where the ground starts descending away from Cathedral, you are heading for The Pope and, shortly after that, for an international border it is illegal to cross here.

The route itself confirms as you go rather than at a single spot: each pitch has a move or two of old-school 5.3 with scrambling between, so seven pitches of mostly-easy ground with occasional short difficulties is CORRECT here and is not a sign you have wandered onto the walk-up. The real crux announces itself — about 400 feet below the summit you cross a DIKE, and the two short pitches immediately above that dike are the hardest climbing on the route. A final airy fourth-class scramble finishes it.

NEGATIVE MARKER for the start: if you find yourself entering a deep gully with a detached tower on your right, you have walked to the SE Buttress start. The NE Ridge is gained from open grassy slope off the main trail, with no gully involved.

Descent is the ordinary walk-up route to the WEST, and a short rappel may be wanted to get off the summit ridge.
hazards: Continuing north along the ridge toward The Pope and the Canadian border
Loose rock on a long broken ridge
Very long walk out from a remote basin if anything goes wrong
A no-fall step-across on the standard walk-off descent

approach_variants.name: Upper Cathedral Lake, round the west side of the water to the Ka'aba Buttress
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Note the wall is north-west facing and stays in shade until around three in the afternoon, so an early start here is a cold one
approach_variants.notes:
Get to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft by whichever of the long trails suits — this is the same basin used for Cathedral Peak, one to two days in from any trailhead.

The climbing is directly above the water, which is why every published approach time is measured in minutes rather than hours: ten to thirty minutes from camp. If you are camped on the north side of the lake, walk around it on the WEST side and straight up to the buttress.

Amphitheater's crags rise above the lake on the far side, and the two named buttresses on that wall are visible from your first sight of the water: Ka'aba on the LEFT, Middle Finger on the RIGHT.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COUNT IS THE TEST. Middle Finger Buttress is the BIGGEST feature on the wall, and Ka'aba — where this route is — sits TWO BUTTRESSES TO ITS LEFT. So find the biggest one first, then count two left. Ka'aba itself is blocky and stepped, described as looking like stepping stones, which is quite unlike the clean sweep of Middle Finger.

Be aware that the two buttresses between them are unnamed in every published source, so the count is the only handle you have — nobody has written a left-to-right inventory of this wall.

Arrival is a LARGE BLOCK at the base that you scramble onto for the first pitch, and getting onto it has a documented seasonal trap. Approaching from the LEFT side of the block runs into a large snow moat that stopped one party in early July. The RIGHT side goes, though it needs some care on friction moves crossing the top of the block to reach the wall.

Walk-off, and there are two. The short one is a gully on the north side about a thousand feet east of Ka'aba, roughly thirty-five to forty degrees, giving a half-mile return to the lake — but it can hold firm snow through July. The longer one circles south around Amphitheater's western arm on sand and then meadows with a decent trail, rejoining the Boundary Trail and returning to the lake in about two miles and fifty minutes of easy walking.
hazards: A snow moat on the left side of the entry block into early July
The north-side descent gully holding firm snow through July
A north-west aspect that stays cold and shaded until mid-afternoon
Very remote — the nearest trailhead is a multi-day walk

approach_variants.name: Robinson Creek #478 to the Beauty Creek trail #579, then the tarn basin
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep on rock. Earlier, with snow on the upper scree, is genuinely easier — the scree is the worst thing about this climb and snow removes it
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Highway 20 west from Winthrop about fifteen miles, right onto Lost River Road, a half mile then left to stay on it, seven and a half paved miles and another mile and a quarter of gravel FR 5400 to the Robinson Creek trailhead on the right. Published trailhead elevations run 2,500 to 2,600 ft. Ballard Campground is a minute or two away and is the standard car-camp.

Walk the Robinson Creek trail #478 — an easy valley walk through big timber — about two and a half miles to the Beauty Creek junction near 3,560 to 3,600 ft. Published mileages for it range from two to two and eight tenths, so use the ELEVATION and the landmark rather than a mile count.

The landmark is the SECOND bridge, the one over Beauty Creek, with Beauty Creek Falls cascading beside it. The junction is thirty to a hundred feet PAST that bridge, on the uphill side, and it is unmarked. Two parties independently warn that it is far less obvious than published beta suggests, one describing it as covered in bushes and nearly walked past. If you get thirty feet beyond the bridge and have not seen it, stop, go back, and look up on climber's right.

Beauty Creek #579 — not #479, which is a different trail entirely — is unmaintained and does not appear on maps. It STAYS ON THE WEST AND NORTH-WEST SIDE OF THE CREEK the whole way. One party notes their topo showed it on the east side and the topo was wrong; that is a usable check. Blowdown is the recurring nuisance, typically five to nine logs.

Total for the peak is fourteen to fifteen miles with somewhere between 6,200 and 6,900 ft of gain, and four separate parties report ten to fourteen hours car to car as a single day.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SECOND TRANSITION IS AN UNBRIDGED CREEK, and five sources put it within sixty vertical feet of each other at about 5,200 to 5,260 ft. That creek is the outflow of the tarn you are heading for. Just a few feet past it the ground opens into meadow. Turn LEFT, north-west, and go up.

The boot path there is easy to miss — one climber walked past it thinking it was where a few goats had gone up the hill. About a hundred feet above the creek it turns into a well-worn track. If you cannot find it, do not hunt: several parties simply climbed north-west through the open meadow and reached the tarn anyway.

NEGATIVE MARKER: if the Beauty Creek trail starts a gradual TRAVERSE below Robinson into the Beauty Creek headwaters, you have gone past the crossing.

ARRIVAL is a small heart-shaped tarn in a rocky basin at about 6,700 to 6,750 ft, sitting between two spur ridges, reached in fifteen hundred feet or so of climbing in well under a mile. This is the standard high camp and it is the LAST WATER — there is none above it.
