Above the tarn the ridge is gained somewhere between 7,400 and 7,600 ft depending on where you take it, up a scree slope that every single source complains about. Carry patience and a helmet; there is a documented near-miss from party-inflicted rockfall here.

THE FALSE SUMMIT IS POINT 8,280 AND IT IS CORROBORATED THREE WAYS. It sits north-west of the tarn, it looks exactly like the top, and the real summit is another HALF MILE beyond it. The test is simple: if you top out and there is more ridge, more gendarmes and a higher point about half a mile to the north-west, you are on the 8,280 south-east peak. It can be sidehilled rather than climbed.

The true crux comes just before the summit: a notch below the last false top, then about fifty to sixty feet of exposed Class 2-3 ridge. Two sources independently say the first five or six feet are the worst of it. Parties carry rock protection and do not place it.

One disambiguation for anyone reading around: Robinson PEAK, above Harts Pass, is a different mountain a mile or so down the ridge from Robinson MOUNTAIN. Harts Pass is not an approach to this climb.
hazards: An unmarked, bushy junction thirty to a hundred feet past the Beauty Creek bridge
Blowdown on an unmaintained trail that is not on maps
No water above the 6,700 ft tarn
A universally loathed scree slope with recorded party-inflicted rockfall — helmet
Fifty to sixty feet of exposed Class 3 just below the summit

approach_variants.name: Slate Pass, the Middle Fork Pasayten, and Fred's Lake to Lake Doris
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the pass above Fred's Lake holds snow on its north side and softens through the day
approach_variants.notes:
Drive FR 5400 from Mazama to Harts Pass, published at 6,181 to 6,204 ft. Trailers are prohibited past the 5400000/5400060 junction because the road is narrow and steep with few turnouts, and whether an ordinary car should attempt it is genuinely disputed in print, so judge it on the day.

From Harts Pass turn right at the guard station onto FR 5400-600. The Pacific Crest Trail trailhead is at the first switchback and SLATE PASS at the second, at about 6,900 ft. Early in the season you walk the last half mile or so.

From Slate Pass take the Buckskin Ridge trail #498, and at about half a mile a cut-off drops to the Robinson Creek / Middle Fork trail #478. Follow the Middle Fork of the Pasayten — an unbridged crossing, reported anywhere from ankle deep to needing boots and trousers off — for roughly nine miles to the Fred's Lake turn-off. The tread through here is in good condition with essentially no brush. Then over the pass to Lake Doris at about 6,975 ft, reported at just under six hours from the car.

A naming caution before you cross-reference maps: this water is Lake Doris in most sources and Lake Dorothy in one. Do not assume they are separate.

Despite the stored route name, every published description of the ordinary way up this peak works the SOUTH or SOUTH-WEST slope, not a west one.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEAVE THE TRAIL AT THE STREAM CROSSING JUST BEFORE THE LAKE, not at the lake. Two independent accounts do exactly that: cross the stream, head north-east up into open forest, and break out of the trees onto talus.

The arrival test is the ground itself. The talus is CONTINUOUS and endless — no benches, no trees, no interruption — running roughly fourteen hundred feet straight to the top. There is no elegant line on it; you put your head down and climb. If you are still weaving between trees and heather benches you have not reached the slope proper.

NEGATIVE MARKER for leaving too early: one climber went up toward what he took to be the south-west ridge, found it was not, and had to work up and down to reach the real one, where bits of use trail run through the least-bad talus. Use-trail fragments are a sign you are on the right slope.

SUMMIT TEST: the top is ringed by cliffs on every side EXCEPT the scree slope you came up. If you are on a summit with more than one walkable side, it is not this one.

HOW TO KNOW IT IS OSCEOLA AND NOT CARRU: Mount Carru is about a mile EAST and it is HIGHER — 8,595 ft against Osceola's 8,587. From the top of Osceola you look east across a deep notch at a higher peak. The ground between the two is described by one climber as somewhere between awful and impassable, so that notch is a wall, not a link. Osceola, Carru and Lago all keep their steep and cliffy ground on the NORTH, which gives a broader check: a peak in this group whose easy ground is on the north side is none of the three.

Nothing published reports a false summit on Osceola.
hazards: Unbridged Middle Fork Pasayten crossing of very variable depth
Blowdown that worsens beyond Fred's Lake, in places hundreds of logs through burn zones
Lingering snow on the north side of the pass above Fred's Lake, soft late in the day
Wet lichen making the talus slippery
Fourteen hundred feet of loose scree with no shelter

approach_variants.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Jackita Ridge #738 and the Crater Lake trail #746
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct; the Canyon Creek ford is the constraint in spring and early summer
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Canyon Creek trailhead at about 1,900 ft on Highway 20 near milepost 141, roughly fifty-five miles west of Winthrop or thirty-three east of Marblemount. Vault toilet, no drinking water.

THERE IS NO BRIDGE OVER CANYON CREEK on Jackita Ridge trail #738, and the Forest Service describes the crossing as difficult and potentially hazardous in spring and early summer. How people get across changes from year to year — one season a shin-deep wade a hundred yards upstream, another a log fifty metres up — so do not plan on a fixed method.

The first mile and a half is brushy. The trail then climbs steeply through timber on a long series of switchbacks to the junction with the Crater Lake trail #746. That junction is UNSIGNED, reported by two separate parties, and its elevation is published as either 5,000 or 5,260 ft.

Turn onto #746 and climb toward Crater Lake. There is a second unmarked junction just before the lake, leading to the old east lookout site; stay with the main path, which runs along the SOUTH shore. Crater Lake is the last water — the ground above is dry, and the lake itself is shallow enough that water filtered at the outlet comes out warm.

The whole peak is commonly given as fourteen to fifteen miles round trip with about 6,300 ft of gain, corroborated by three independent sources.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There are three markers above the lake and they come in order.

FIRST, at about 6,800 ft the grade mellows and the trail turns north. Two parties record the same elevation for it.

SECOND, at about 7,600 ft THE TRAIL ENDS — it does not fade, it disappears into a loose gully, and three sources agree on the height. That is where the scrambling starts.

THIRD, and this is the thing you can see: the gully is marked by a downscoping RIBBON OF WHITE ROCK and the first of several yellow painted X marks. One climber calls it pretty hard to miss once you know to look for it.

NEGATIVE MARKER, and it is important because the marking itself is the trap: the paint tempts you straight UP that gully. It starts well and turns steep and loose with rolling pebbles higher up. A party who followed the paint up found on the way down that the better line TRAVERSES ACROSS the gully and around the corner, where cairns lead upward. Once you reach a yellow ARROW, the ground improves markedly for the rest of the way.

HOW YOU KNOW YOU HAVE FINISHED THE HARD PART, corroborated four ways and genuinely reassuring: the scrambling ENDS well below the summit and real trail resumes. A mellow path runs the last quarter mile to the top, past the remnants of an old tramway at the top of the cliff section. If you are still scrambling within sight of the summit, you are off the line.

There is one false top, a bump on the south ridge, and the trail bypasses it to the WEST — the real summit sits directly behind it and is not visible from below.

Two things to have straight before you go, because both are commonly stated wrongly. The historic lookout stood on the HIGHEST summit, not a lower one; the second, lower lookout site is on a peak about a mile EAST. And the lookout tender here was Gary Snyder in 1952 — Jack Kerouac was on Desolation Peak, a different mountain some fifteen miles away, four years later. The summit register itself carries a card that conflates the two.
hazards: An unbridged Canyon Creek ford, hazardous in spring and early summer, with no fixed crossing point
Yellow paint marks that lead into a steep, loose gully rather than along the better line
Loose rock through the scramble section, reported by most parties
No water above Crater Lake
Broken glass and nails around the old lookout remains on the east peak

approach_variants.name: Devils Dome loop from the East Bank trailhead
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, as a multi-day trip
approach_variants.notes:
A genuinely different approach with a specific purpose: it EXISTS TO AVOID THE CANYON CREEK FORD. The party who wrote it up said so directly, having judged a day trip from Canyon Creek to involve a difficult crossing at the time they were there.

It starts from the East Bank trailhead near Ruby Creek and runs roughly forty-eight miles with about 13,100 ft of gain over three days, taking in Devils Dome. That is a very different undertaking from the day-trip standard, and it is chosen for access rather than for the mountain.

Nothing is published on a Granite Creek or East Creek approach, so do not assume one exists.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The summit end of the day is the same regardless of how you got into the basin: the trail dies around 7,600 ft into a loose gully marked by a ribbon of white rock and a yellow X, the paint leads you up rather than across, and the scrambling finishes well below the top where real trail resumes for the last quarter mile.

What differs is your bearing on arrival. Coming round by Devils Dome you meet the peak from the north-east rather than up from Crater Lake, so identify the south-ridge false top and the white ribbon from a distance before dropping into the basin, rather than expecting to walk into them off a known trail.
hazards: A three-day committing loop with substantial cumulative gain
Same loose gully and misleading paint above
Long stretches with no bail-out
